thread.title: The Apple 'Disaster': 7% Earnings Growth And $20 Billion In An Irish Bank - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)

author: Trading Places Research
title: The Apple 'Disaster': 7% Earnings Growth And $20 Billion In An Irish Bank - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)
text:
That feeling when graffiti makes more sense than floor traders. By cogdogblog - Good Advice , CC0, Bring a towel, too.
Apple at $100? Yes, Please. When Apple ( AAPL ) was still around $200, I wrote an article titled “ Apple at $150? Yes, Please. ” The point of the article was that I had such faith in Apple’s long-term prospects (and I gave thirteen reasons why), that I was willing to absorb large losses and just buy more when I felt everyone had stopped losing their minds. Usually, regaining losses has been a matter of a quarter or two. “Buy Apple on the dip,” is the best advice I’ve ever given, and I will continue to give it until it stops working. I bought some more at $150.
I am not a fan of 'This Time It’s Different', but this time is different. The timing couldn’t be worse, with The Bull and The Bear engaged in thermonuclear war for supremacy. The animal spirits are out, and they were already coming for Apple to begin with, so this is a steamroller that could really take Apple down several notches before it recovers. Who knows where this ends.
But as we will see, this $5 billion shortfall in revenue actually translates into 7% earnings growth and another $20 billion in an Irish bank. Not so bad for a disaster.
Thank God for Shareholder Lawsuits Did I just say that out loud? I hate shareholder lawsuits, which are frivolous 90% of the time. But a nice by-product is Tim Cook’s letter to shareholders after close on the first day of 2019 trading.
In an article published just hours before the letter, I jokingly compared Apple’s secrecy between SEC filings to the Soviet Politburo. This letter is a highly unusual early peek into an Apple quarter, and I can only guess that the lawyers insisted they do it to fend off lawsuits. Note it came the day after the quarter ended, a schedule I am guessing the lawyers insisted on. Lawyers are so thoughtful that way.
Anyway, to the maths!
Revenue of approximately $84 billion Gross margin of approximately 38 percent Operating expenses of approximately $8.7 billion Other income/(expense) of approximately $550 million Tax rate of approximately 16.5 percent before discrete items So:
$84 billion times 38% equals $31.92 billion $31.92 billion minus $8.7 billion equals $23.22 billion $23.22 billion plus $550 million equals $23.77 billion Paying taxes on $23.77 billion leaves $19.85 billion The average share count in the quarter was 4.77 billion $19.85 billion divided by 4.77 billion shares is $4.16, an almost 7% improvement over the year-ago quarter. Apple’s disastrous quarter that has already wiped out a third of its value actually shows earnings growth that is far from awful. And another $20 billion in an Irish bank that will go into bringing down the share count even further.
Disaster!
Some Context As I write this, Apple sits at $146 after-hours. We now know they will earn around $4.16 per share in Q1, bringing their TTM earnings up to $12.15. Its TTM PE is 12.02. Its cash-net-debt is about $26/share. So minus the cash, the market is currently valuing Apple at $120, 9.88x earnings. Shareholder equity (i.e., the liquidation value of Apple) is over $22/share, so minus shareholder equity, the market is pricing Apple at 10.16x earnings. Come on, now.
But, This Is The Bad News The bad news is, this is the first time a macro shock has affected Apple's revenue in the post iPhone era. People can say all they want, but Tim Cook used the word “China” 11 times and every one of them was aimed at the President. The lawyers may have dictated that he send this letter on the first day after the quarter ended, but his message was clear: the President of the United States is messing with our business, and we are not the first nor the last.
Their SEC filing will likely show continued strong revenue everywhere but China.
But more to the point - look how Apple did through the last recession, the last time it was hit with a macro shock:
AAPL data by YCharts
The stock got batted around, but revenue and earnings per share grew quickly, and the share price eventually caught up. But that was the early days of the iPhone, so they could more easily absorb the macro shock because they were opening up new markets.
Now it is clear that they can’t just sponge up the negative effects of the world's largest economy trying to destroy the world’s second largest economy the way they did in 2008-2009 crisis.
In my Q4 Outlook I joked that:
Be very afraid of the following phrases in Q3/Q4 earnings calls:
"Rising costs from tariffs" "Rising costs from inflation" "Increased labor costs" "Rising interest rates" Any mention of China Any of the above will be good for an analyst downgrade.
Now we know this also applies to Apple.
So What Can Apple Do? Well, the first thing is to lobby the President to end the trade war, which this letter already does.
But beyond that.
Apple clearly needs to diversify their revenue away from the iPhone, and they are also doing that. They can also continue to make their pitch vs. Android on security and privacy, and they are already doing that. No one is better at pulling revenue and earnings levers than Tim Cook and Jeff Williams. I believe the iPhone buyback promotion was not only to juice sales of new phones but also to leverage the high resale value of the trade-ins . Finally, India. India has 1.3 billion people and very few of them have an iPhone. Do you know why? I don’t. It is the only large market where the iPhone is completely uncompetitive and not a huge object of luxury desire. Going from zero to 5% market share in India would make a huge difference to Apple, especially in directing their EM exposure away from China.
I may not understand Apple’s Indian difficulties, but I bet Tim Cook has a few thoughts, as he’s been alluding to this issue for a while now. The first step has already been announced. Many people are interpreting the new Apple Foxconn factory in India to be about moving production away from China, and it is. But it is also about moving it to India, and hopefully selling Indian-made iPhones to Indians.
Implications for the Stock My best advice has always been “buy Apple on the dip” and it’s worked for some time now, and it will continue to work until it doesn’t. I still rate it my best advice.
But this dip is different. The timing and the resonance of the news with existing trade war fears is like a triple whammy to sentiment, which I consider very negative to begin with. The stock will likely open way down on Thursday, and could hit free fall before it finds bottom. In the current environment, it could even go as low as $100 in January, and I will of course buy more there.
Never try and call the bottom, because the market can stay irrational longer than you can stay solvent, especially in times like these. Apple will be fine. They are the best run and largest company in the world, and they have $120 billion in cash with which to solve problems. They were already working on solving the Chinese problem before we even knew there was a Chinese problem.
Sadly... My policy with heavily-followed companies like Apple is to not read or respond to comments, as they seem to attract a large amount of FUD and trolling. Feel free to send me a private message if you have a question or comment directed at me. If you are polite and respectful, you will almost certainly get a response that is also polite and respectful.
